slide.heading: Breathe In
slide.subheading: Getting air in, and oxygen across

lines.text: Good morning. I'm Priya Raman, pulmonology. Take a deep breath. That breath cost you almost nothing, and today we find out why.
Two problems: getting air in and out, which is mechanics, and getting oxygen across into the blood, which is gas exchange.
This afternoon you'll measure your own lungs in the spirometry lab, so pay attention to the volumes.

slide.heading: Lung volumes and capacities
bullets: Tidal volume ≈ 500 mL at rest
Residual volume: what you can never breathe out
FRC = expiratory reserve + residual volume
Spirometry can't measure RV, FRC or TLC
TLC = vital capacity + residual volume

lines.text: At rest you move about half a litre per breath: the tidal volume. You could breathe in about three litres more, or out about one more.
But you can never empty your lungs. What's left is the residual volume, and it can't be measured by a spirometer, because you can't blow it out.
At the end of a quiet breath, the lungs' inward recoil and the chest wall's outward spring balance. The volume there is the functional residual capacity: expiratory reserve plus residual volume.
Add the residual volume to the vital capacity and you have the total lung capacity.

slide.heading: Spirometry: obstructive or restrictive?
bullets: FVC: everything you can blow out
FEV1: how much in the first second
Obstructive (asthma, COPD): FEV1/FVC < 0.7
Restrictive (fibrosis): small volumes, ratio normal or high
Confirm restriction with TLC

lines.text: Blow out as hard and fast as you can, all the way. The total is the forced vital capacity; the amount in the first second is the FEV1.
In asthma and COPD the airways are narrowed, so air comes out slowly: the FEV1 falls much more than the FVC, and the ratio drops below point seven.
In fibrosis the lungs are small and stiff. Both numbers fall, but the ratio stays normal or even rises. To prove restriction you need the total lung capacity.

slide.heading: Compliance and surfactant
bullets: Compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure
Fibrosis: stiff, low compliance
Emphysema: floppy, high compliance, poor recoil
Surfactant (type II cells) lowers surface tension
Premature babies lack it: respiratory distress syndrome

lines.text: How easily do the lungs stretch? That's compliance: change in volume over change in pressure.
Fibrosis makes them stiff. Emphysema destroys elastic tissue, so they're easy to inflate but recoil poorly, and air gets trapped.
And the alveoli are wet, so surface tension tries to collapse them, most of all the small ones. Surfactant, made by type two pneumocytes, lowers the tension and keeps them open.

slide.heading: Matching air to blood
bullets: Overall V/Q ≈ 0.8
Shunt (V/Q = 0): blood passes unventilated alveoli
Shunt hypoxemia barely improves with 100% O₂
Dead space (V/Q = ∞): ventilated, not perfused
A pulmonary embolus creates dead space

lines.text: Oxygen only gets in where air and blood meet. Ventilation and perfusion have to match.
If blood flows past alveoli that aren't ventilated, full of pus or collapsed, it comes back unoxygenated. That's a shunt, and giving more oxygen barely helps, because it never reaches that blood.
The opposite is dead space: ventilated alveoli with no blood flow, as beyond a pulmonary embolus.

slide.heading: Hemoglobin: loading and unloading
bullets: Sigmoidal: cooperative binding
P50 ≈ 27 mmHg
Right shift: ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑temperature
Right shift unloads O₂ in working tissue
Left shift: fetal Hb, CO, cold, alkalosis

lines.text: Once oxygen is in the blood, hemoglobin carries it. Its binding is cooperative, so the curve is an S, and half-saturated at a PO2 of about twenty-seven.
In working muscle there's more carbon dioxide, more acid, more heat and more 2,3-BPG. Each shifts the curve to the right, and hemoglobin lets its oxygen go exactly where it's needed.
Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly, a left shift, so it can take oxygen from the mother's blood.

slide.heading: The A–a gradient
bullets: PAO₂ = FiO₂ (760 − 47) − PaCO₂ / 0.8
On room air: PAO₂ ≈ 150 − 1.25 × PaCO₂
Normal A–a gradient: about 5–15 mmHg (rises with age)
Hypoventilation: low PaO₂, normal gradient
V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion: high gradient

lines.text: Here's the bedside tool that ties it together. From the arterial blood gas you can estimate the alveolar oxygen with the alveolar gas equation.
The difference between alveolar and arterial oxygen is the A–a gradient. Normally it's small.
If a patient is hypoxemic only because they're hypoventilating, the gradient stays normal. If the problem is in the lung itself, it widens.
